specs.buildable:
PARTIALLY. Two different answers for the two geometries in this paper.

(1) The topology-optimised cold plate (the headline geometry) is NOT buildable from the numbers alone. The four-layer stack is fully specified in Z: silicon die 550 um, TIM 50 um, copper base 300 um, channel layer 800 um, total 1700 um of modelled stack, on a 20 mm x 32.5 mm footprint. The channel depth is 800 um everywhere. What is missing is the in-plane channel layout itself: the design is a converged density field thresholded to a black-and-white pixel image, and the paper publishes only a statistical summary of it (channel width min 90.37 um, mode 134.74 um, mean 186.12 um, max 370.93 um, beta-shaped distribution) plus a picture of one quarter (Fig. 2a). A width histogram does not fix channel centrelines, branching topology, fin shapes or counts, so any CAD built from these numbers would be a different geometry with a similar width statistic. Also missing: cold plate footprint as distinct from chip footprint; inlet port width/length/diameter and its exact coordinate; outlet port cross-section and extent along the left and right edges; the hotspot footprints and coordinates (so the power map cannot be reconstructed either, only its total of 738.66 W and its 400 W/cm2 peak); fin thickness and pitch anywhere in the optimised field; the cartesian design grid resolution. CONCLUSION: to replicate this exactly you must re-run a topology optimisation with their objective (minimise max junction temperature) and their constraints (150 mbar, 1.5 LPM/kW), or digitise Fig. 2a - both are reconstructions, not the paper's geometry.

(2) The seven straight-channel baselines ARE buildable and watertight from stated numbers: equal channel and fin widths of 200, 175, 150, 125, 100, 75 and 50 um (so pitch 400, 350, 300, 250, 200, 150, 100 um by arithmetic, not stated as such), cut into the 800 um channel layer over a 300 um copper base, under a 50 um TIM and a 550 um silicon die, across 20 mm x 32.5 mm. Channel length is NOT_STATED, but the split-flow routing means a channel runs from the vertical centreline out to one side edge, i.e. the 20 mm direction; I am NOT asserting 10 mm because the paper does not state it and the cold plate footprint is not given. Inlet and outlet port geometry is NOT_STATED for these too, so the ports must be chosen by the modeller. RECOMMENDATION: build target (2) as the verifiable case - it reproduces the green benchmark curve of Fig. 4 and the 125 um best-straight-channel reference point - and treat target (1) as a TO problem statement rather than a geometry to copy.
specs.operating_point:
Driving condition is a prescribed pressure drop between inlet and outlet, not a prescribed flow rate. "we conduct simulations for a range of pressure drops: 100, 150, 200, 250 and 300 mbar."

Design constraints: "a pressure drop of 150 mbar and a flow rate per power of 1.5 LPM/kW inside the microfluidic design (1.11 LPM for 738.66 W)". Junction temperature acceptance target: "any junction temperature below 85 C is considered acceptable". The 150 mbar microfluidic budget was set so the whole loop (including 90 degree elbows at the out-of-plane inlet/outlets, filters, valves, connectors) stays under 300 mbar.

Nominal operating point of the optimised design: 150 mbar, flow rate 1.09 LPM, which the paper notes "corresponds to 1.47 LPM/kW". Lower-power operating point also reported: the 85 C target "is reached by the hotspot-aware design at just 100 mbar and 0.79 LPM."

Heat load: total power 738.66 W over the 20 mm x 32.5 mm die (area 6.5 cm2), applied as a heterogeneous power map heat flux at the junction face (the silicon face away from the cold plate), with four hotspots at 400 W/cm2 each. Side walls adiabatic.

Coolant: water with 25% propylene glycol, inlet temperature 25 C, thermal conductivity 0.478 W/mK, dynamic viscosity 0.00286 Pa s, specific heat capacity 3980 J/kgK. Coolant DENSITY IS NOT_STATED. REYNOLDS NUMBER IS NOT_STATED anywhere in the paper, and cannot be computed without the density.

Solid properties: silicon 150 W/mK, TIM 8.5 W/mK (phase change material), copper 400 W/mK.

Single phase, conjugate heat transfer, Navier-Stokes with a Brinkman term during optimisation; the final evaluation is body-fitted high-fidelity CFD.
specs.reported_results:
Optimised (hotspot-aware) design at 150 mbar / 1.09 LPM:
- Maximum junction temperature 81.19 C, at four distinct hotspots of 81.19 C each; "just below the initial target of 85 C".
- Junction temperature rise 56.19 K above the 25 C inlet.
- Maximum copper fin temperature inside the microfluidic heat sink 48.99 C.
- Maximum temperature at the cold plate layer 53.21 C; at the TIM layer 63.61 C; at the junction layer 81.19 C (three-level stack-up of the conductive drop).
- Maximum coolant velocity 3.71 m/s inside the copper cold plate.
- Optimised design also meets the 85 C target at 100 mbar / 0.79 LPM.

Versus straight channels:
- "over the entire evaluated range of pressures, the hotpot-aware cooling design outperforms any straight parallel microchannel design by a 12.69% reduction in temperature rise or a 55% reduction in pressure drop for the same temperature rise." Conclusions round this to "almost 13%" / "55% reduction in pressure drop ... within 150 mbar".
- Within the 1.5 LPM/kW and 150 mbar constraints the best straight channel is the 125 um design; against it the optimised design gives "a 9.14% reduction of the junction temperature, which corresponds to an absolute decrease of 8.17 C."
- For pressures below 300 mbar, the 100 um straight channels give the lowest temperature rise among the straight designs.
- Only the 75, 100 and 125 um straight designs reach 85 C at all, and only marginally, needing more than 200 mbar and/or more than 1.11 LPM.
- 50 um straight channels have a junction temperature higher than 105 C.

NOT REPORTED anywhere in the paper: Nusselt number, heat transfer coefficient, thermal resistance in K/W or K cm2/W, friction factor, pumping power, per-design tabulated numbers behind Fig. 4 (only the plot), and any experimental data - "Future work will focus on manufacturing and experimental evaluation of the cold plates to validate this performance increase." So the checkable targets are the temperatures, the 3.71 m/s peak velocity, and the 1.09 LPM at 150 mbar.
specs.mesh_used:
POORLY SPECIFIED - treat as NOT_STATED for any grid-convergence purpose.

Optimisation stage: two PDEs "adapted to the 2.5D framework described in [1]" solved by the Finite Element Method using the open-source package Firedrake; hydrodynamics is Navier-Stokes augmented with a Brinkman term, with hydrodynamic resistance derived from the density field; conjugate heat transfer solved across all four layers; design variables are a density scalar field in [0,1] "on a piecewise constant function space defined on a cartesian grid". The cartesian grid resolution, element count and element type are NOT_STATED. Convergence is reported only as iteration count: "the evolution of the TO that converges to an optimized geometry after 200 iterations", with frames shown at iterations 10, 20, 30, 100 and 200. Post-processing applies a 0.5 threshold to the density field plus a cleanup step for "imperfections and geometry anomalies".

Verification stage: "we construct a body-fitted mesh based on the black and white image of the generated geometry and we perform high fidelity thermal Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) by applying a pressure drop between inlet(s) and outlet." The mesher name, cell count, cell type (tet/hex/poly), boundary-layer or prism-layer treatment, near-wall resolution, y+ and turbulence model (if any) are all NOT_STATED. NO GRID CONVERGENCE / MESH INDEPENDENCE STUDY IS PRESENTED, and no solver validation against experiment. This is the single biggest gap for anyone trying to reproduce their numbers: the 81.19 C and 1.09 LPM at 150 mbar cannot be mesh-matched, only approached.

This report contains the SAME three water-cooled etched silicon microchannel heat sinks reported in the 1981 letter (samples 80D6, 80D19, 81F9), with far more geometric detail than the 4-page letter carries. The link is proven by the 1981 abstract's own headline numbers: the letter reports 790 W/cm2 and a 71 C substrate rise; UCRL-53515 Table 3-5 gives sample 81F9 at q" = 790 W/cm2 with R = 0.090 cm2.C/W, and 790 x 0.090 = 71.1 C.

INDEPENDENT CROSS-CHECK of the headline design, read in full: W. Qu and I. Mudawar, "Analysis of three-dimensional heat transfer in micro-channel heat sinks", Int. J. Heat Mass Transfer 45 (2002) 3973-3985, https://engineering.purdue.edu/mudawar/files/articles-all/2002/2002_3.pdf - citing Tuckerman and Pease [3] = the 1981 EDL letter: "Tuckerman and Pease [3] fabricated a micro-channel heat sink by chemically etching parallel channels in a 1-cm2 silicon wafer. The channels had a width of 50 um and a depth of 302 um, and were separated by 50 um thick walls." That matches sample 81F9 exactly (50 um wide, 302 um deep, 100 um pitch so 50 um walls), confirming 81F9 is the design the 1981 letter is famous for.

specs.buildable:
YES for the canonical design (sample 81F9) and for designs 80D6 and 80D19, with ONE assumption you must record, plus ONE documented conflict.

WHAT IS FULLY SPECIFIED (81F9): channel width 50 um, channel depth 302 um, fin/wall thickness 50 um, pitch 100 um, channel length 1.40 cm, channel-array width 2.0 cm, total silicon thickness 458 um, residual silicon base under the channel floors 156 um (= 458 - 302, using the report's own definition H_s = t_Si - H), rectangular channel cross-section with flat floor and vertical walls, Pyrex cover plate 0.8 mm (Table 3-1) or 1.0 mm (body text), two 3 mm x 16 mm rectangular through-slots in that cover plate as inlet and outlet manifolds with ~5 degrees of sandblast draft, overall bonded laminate outline 25.4 mm x 34.5 mm, heat-source patch 1 cm x 1 cm on the opposite (front) face.

BUILD RECIPE: take a 34.5 x 34.5 mm silicon block 458 um thick. On the back face, cut a 2.0 cm wide x 1.40 cm long array of rectangular grooves, each 50 um wide x 302 um deep, on a 100 um pitch, with the grooves terminating inside the silicon (blind at both ends, no breakout to the die edge). Cap with a flat Pyrex plate 0.8 mm thick carrying two 3 x 16 mm through-slots that land over the two ends of the groove array. Trim the bonded stack to 25.4 x 34.5 mm. Put the 1 cm x 1 cm heat source centred on the front face. The fluid domain is the groove void plus the two slot volumes; the solid domain is the silicon (156 um base + 302 um tall fins) plus the Pyrex.

THE ONE ASSUMPTION: channel count n is NOT_STATED. Do not hard-code it. Sweep the stated 100 um pitch across the stated 2.0 cm array width and let the count emerge (that gives 200, but the report never writes 200). Equivalently, model one 100 um periodic unit cell (50 um fluid + 25 um of silicon on each side) and apply symmetry, which is how the report itself analyses it.

THE ONE CONFLICT: Pyrex cover-plate thickness is 0.8 mm in Table 3-1 step 9 and 1 mm in the body text on p.64. Both are quoted above. The report never reconciles them. It only affects the manifold slot depth, so it changes header pressure drop slightly and nothing in the channel core. Pick 0.8 mm (the process spec) and flag it.

WHAT IS GENUINELY MISSING AND WOULD NEED AN ASSUMPTION: (1) the in-plane POSITION of the two manifold slots on the cover plate - the report gives slot size and channel length but never the slot centres; place them so the open channel run between the inner slot edges equals the stated 1.40 cm. (2) The runout distance from each blind groove end to the die edge. (3) The position of the 1 cm x 1 cm heater patch relative to the 1.40 cm channel array - the report says only that the array is deliberately larger so registration is 'noncritical', and that temperature was probed at x = 9 mm; centring the heater on the array is the natural reading but is not stated. (4) Fillet radii at the groove corners - none given; KOH-etched <110> grooves are modelled as sharp rectangles, which is what the report's own Fig. 3-19 does.

DO NOT MODEL the 400 um figure as a channel depth: that is the process etch target in Table 3-1 step 7, not an as-built dimension. The as-built depths are 287, 302 and 320 um.

ONE MORE CAUTION FOR THE CAD: sample 81D7C3 in the same table (0.083 cm2.C/W at 1309 W/cm2, the best number in the whole report) is a SAWN PIN-FIN part, 55 um pins on a 90 um pitch, 400 um tall, and it is NOT one of the 1981 letter's straight-channel designs. Do not mix it into a straight-parallel-channel model.
specs.operating_point:
COOLANT: water. UCRL-53515 p.69: 'Deionized water was supplied to a precision pressure regulator', filtered through a '15-um filter (Nupro SS-4F-15)'. Resistivity 18 Mohm. Fluid properties are NOT tabulated in the report; it works from standard water property correlations and notes the viscosity drops with temperature ('the viscosity of the water decreases with increasing temperature', p.81-82).

COOLANT INLET TEMPERATURE: NOT_STATED for the three heat-sink runs. The 1981 letter's abstract reports temperature rise 'above the input water temperature' without giving that temperature. The only inlet temperature stated anywhere in UCRL-53515 is for a separate long-duration erosion test: p.86, 'Deionized water (18 Mohm, 18 C), filtered to better than 15 um, flowed continuously through sample 83MR31E'. Do not apply 18 C to 81F9 without flagging it. The theoretical optimum of Section 2.1.2.1 is stated as 'room-temperature water-cooled'.

PER-DESIGN OPERATING POINTS, all from UCRL-53515 Table 3-5, p.81 (verified against page scan leaf99), each at the maximum tested power:

DESIGN C, sample 81F9 (the canonical one, matches the 1981 letter's headline): pressure drop P = 31 psi (= 2.14 bar = 214 kPa); volume flow rate f = 8.6 cm3/sec (= 8.6 mL/s = 0.516 L/min); heat flux q" = 790 W/cm2 over the 1 cm x 1 cm heater, i.e. 790 W total.

DESIGN B, sample 80D19: P = 17 psi (= 1.17 bar); f = 6.5 cm3/sec; q" = 277 W/cm2.

DESIGN A, sample 80D6: P = 15 psi (= 1.03 bar); f = 4.7 cm3/sec; q" = 181 W/cm2.

FLOW SPLIT CAVEAT, essential if you compare CFD to the reported numbers. The cold plate is wider than the heater, so not all the measured flow passes under the heat source. UCRL-53515 p.80: 'This discrepancy between the cold-plate area and the smaller heated area implies that not all the input flow is effective in cooling. For example, if W_s = 1.5 cm whereas W = 1.0 cm, then approximately 2/3 of the coolant flows underneath the heater resistor.' For 81F9, W_s = 2.0 cm against a 1.0 cm heater, so roughly half the tabulated 8.6 cm3/sec is under the heater. The report corrects for this with f_hot = f_cold - (1 - W/W_s) f_cold.

REYNOLDS NUMBER: NOT_STATED for 80D6, 80D19 or 81F9. Related stated values, for different samples: Table 3-3 p.79 gives 'Maximum Re' of 330 and 390 for etched plate-fin samples 83MR31E and 83MY16B, and 900 for sawn sample 82AP26C1; Table 3-4 p.80 gives 900, 700 and 760 for pin-fin samples. p.80 notes 'the Reynolds numbers tested (up to 900)'. For the theoretical optimum, p.26: 'Re = 5.42(...)^(1/4) ~ 1560 under the stated conditions, hence the flow will indeed be laminar.' The flow regime throughout is single-phase laminar.

DESIGN-INTENT OPERATING POINT (not an as-tested one): p.82, 'the design value of ~10 cm3/sec'; Section 2.1.2.1 designs at 'a water pressure of P = 50 psi = 3.45X10^6 dynes/cm2'. The package 'was operated continuously at 50 psi for over a month without problems' (p.64).

MEASUREMENT LOCATION: UCRL-53515 p.80, 'measuring temperature T at the 90% downstream location (x = 9 mm)'. All Table 3-5 resistances are maximum (downstream) values, not averages. Match this probe point when comparing CFD.

All thermal resistances below are AREA-NORMALISED, units cm2.C/W, defined in UCRL-53515 nomenclature p.xiii as 'R = LW theta, thermal resistance normalized to unit area'. Because the heater is exactly 1 cm2, the numeric value in cm2.C/W equals the plain C/W for these parts.

From UCRL-53515 Table 3-5, p.81, 'Maximum (downstream) thermal resistance of various silicon microchannel heat sinks at maximum tested power' (verified twice: OCR text and the page scan):

DESIGN C, sample 81F9 (CANONICAL): R = 0.090 cm2.C/W at q" = 790 W/cm2, 31 psi, 8.6 cm3/sec. Cross-check against the 1981 letter's own abstract: 'At a power density of 790 W/cm2, a maximum substrate temperature rise of 71 C above the input water temperature was measured, in good agreement with theory.' 790 W/cm2 x 0.090 cm2.C/W = 71.1 C. This closes the loop between the two documents exactly.

DESIGN B, sample 80D19: R = 0.113 cm2.C/W at q" = 277 W/cm2, 17 psi, 6.5 cm3/sec. Implied rise 277 x 0.113 = 31.3 C.

DESIGN A, sample 80D6: R = 0.110 cm2.C/W at q" = 181 W/cm2, 15 psi, 4.7 cm3/sec. Implied rise 181 x 0.110 = 19.9 C.

CONTEXT ROWS FROM THE SAME TABLE, NOT part of the 1981 letter's straight-channel set: sample 82A26C1 (etched plate fin, w_c 64 um, H 280 um): R = 0.280 at 34.6 W/cm2, 15 psi, 1.86 cm3/sec. Sample 81D7C3 (SAWN PIN-FIN, 55 um pins, 90 um pitch, H 400 um): R = 0.083 at 1309 W/cm2, 53 psi, 14.2 cm3/sec - the best number in the report, and the one behind the abstract's '0.083 C/W'. UCRL-53515 abstract: 'Thermal resistances as low as 0.083 C/W were measured from 1-cm2 thin-film resistors (e.g., a 108 C temperature rise at' 1309 W/cm2.

SCALED EXTRAPOLATION the authors give, useful as a second CFD target: UCRL-53515 p.80: 'we could extrapolate the performance of sample 81F9 to R = 0.077 cm2.C/W and that of sample 81D7C3 to R = 0.067 cm2.C/W for the case where L_s = 1.0 cm and P = 30 psi; this requires scaling down all dimensions by (L/L_s)^(1/3).' The handicap being corrected: 'the use of a substrate length which is longer than the 1-cm channel width (L_s >= 1.4 cm in our samples) has handicapped us somewhat. Since optimized thermal resistance scales as L^(1/3) for constant pressure'.

THEORY TARGET: UCRL-53515 p.26, for the optimum 1 cm x 1 cm design at 50 psi, 'theta_opt = 0.055 C/W'. Correlation used: Nu_L = 8.882 after correcting for thermal entrance effects, from solving L/(D Re Pr) = 1/(12 Nu) graphically (Fig. 2-3). Governing relation: Eq. (2.31), theta_opt = (4/3) theta_conv = 2.95 (mu Phi / k_f Nu k_s^3 w^2 rho C P)^(1/3). Decomposition for comparing against CFD, Eq. (3-2): R(x) = R_cond + R_conv(x) + R_cal(x), with R_cal(x) = x W / (rho C f).

NUSSELT NUMBER: no measured Nu is tabulated. The report reports thermal resistance, not Nu. Nu values quoted are theory inputs: Nu_inf for a fully developed profile from Fig. 2-4 as a function of aspect ratio, corrected for entrance effects via Fig. 2-3; Nu_L = 8.882 for the optimum design; Keyes' approximation gives Nu ~ 8.235.

PRESSURE DROP / FLOW FRICTION, for validating the hydraulic side. UCRL-53515 Table 3-3, p.79, plate-fin samples, flow-friction parameter Phi = C_f Re: etched sample 83MR31E, Phi experimental 20.8 +/- 1.1 against 20.0 theory; etched 83MY16B, 20.6 +/- 1.1 against 19.9; sawn 82AP26C1, 19.6 +/- 1.0 against 18.6. Header loss coefficient K measured 2.6 to 5.3 against a theoretical expectation of about 1.6: p.33, 'K ~ 1.6, in fact we have measured K to be between 3 and 4.5, probably because the header' geometry is imperfect. The report's own summary, p.79: 'the experimental flow-friction characteristics of microscopic silicon plate-fin heat sinks are as predicted by theory, except that the header losses appear to be somewhat larger than expected'. NOTE Phi and K are NOT tabulated for 80D6, 80D19 or 81F9 specifically.

BOILING LIMIT, for context: operating one sample into subcooled boiling at f = 0.35 cm3/sec, 'Energy calculations suggest that 15% of the water is being vaporized at burnout' (p.82), with a burnout margin of 'a factor of 2 beyond the initial boiling'.

ACCURACY: channel depth +/- 5 um; pressure gauges 0.25% of full scale (15, 30 or 60 psi FS); current sense resistor +/- 0.25%; surface temperature by movable copper-constantan beaded-junction thermocouple. A heater sheet-resistance gradient of 'up to 2.9%/cm' is corrected for, and is valid 'provided such measurements are made at the center of the thin-film heater'.
specs.mesh_used:
NO MESH. NOT_STATED, and not applicable: there is no CFD in either document. This is a 1981/1984 experimental and analytical study that predates practical CFD for this problem, which is exactly why it is the canonical validation case rather than a simulation to be reproduced.

WHAT WAS DONE INSTEAD OF MESHING. The analysis in UCRL-53515 Chapter 2 is closed-form one-dimensional fin theory coupled to laminar duct correlations, with no discretised domain anywhere. The ingredients, all from UCRL-53515:

1. Thermal resistance split three ways, Eq. (3-2), p.82: R(x) = R_cond + R_conv(x) + R_cal(x), where R_cond = conduction through the residual silicon base, R_conv = convection into the coolant through the finned and prime surfaces, R_cal = caloric rise of the coolant along the channel.
2. Convection from a fin-efficiency treatment: 'eta = combined temperature effectiveness of finned and prime surfaces' and 'eta_f = temperature fin effectiveness factor (finned area)', with normalised fin height m = H sqrt(Nu L k_f / A w_c) per Eq. (2.16).
3. Nusselt number taken from a chart, not computed on a grid: 'Nu_inf is evaluated from Fig. 2-4 for an equivalent rectangular aspect ratio. A correction factor is then applied for thermal entrance effects, using Fig. 2-3' (p.83).
4. Two bracketing variants are carried through rather than one answer: an 'optimistic theory' with R_cal(x) = x W / (rho C f) and a 'conservative theory' with R_cal = x W / (eta rho C f), and the measured points are expected to land between them: 'Here the optimistic and conservative theories are both shown and, as expected, the data generally fit between them' (p.84).
5. Nonlinear corrections applied by hand at high power: 'In the case of large power fluxes (and hence high temperatures), [Nu] is also corrected for the nonlinear viscosity effects, as described in Section 2.2.4' (p.83).
6. Groove cross-section handled by swapping wetted perimeters, not by remeshing: Fig. 3-19, p.83, 'Model of sawn grooves (circular bottoms), etched grooves (square bottoms)', with p_prime evaluated per case.

GRID CONVERGENCE: none, and none possible. There is no grid. The validation evidence offered in its place is a parameter sweep against theory with no fitted constants: p.84, 'Fig. 3-20 plots theory and experiment for sample 82A26A2 at several different flow rates and positions, correlated in terms of the dimensionless axial position x* = x/(D Re Pr) ... The agreement with theory is quite good, in view of the fact that no adjustable parameters were used.'

IF YOU ARE MESHING THIS YOURSELF: the geometry is a conjugate heat transfer problem over one 100 um periodic unit cell (50 um of water plus 25 um of silicon on each side for 81F9), 302 um tall channel on a 156 um silicon base, 14 mm long, with symmetry planes down the channel centreline and the fin centreline. Resolve the thermal entrance region: the report puts the design point at L/(D Re Pr) = 1/(12 Nu) = 0.010, i.e. 'an almost fully-developed temperature profile' but not fully developed, so an entrance-length-resolving streamwise grading matters more than cross-sectional refinement. The report's own cell count, element type and mesher: NOT_STATED, because none exist.

specs.buildable:
PARTIALLY. A watertight FLUID solid is buildable today for all five cases; a watertight CONJUGATE (fluid + solid) assembly is NOT, because one dimension is missing.

BUILDABLE NOW - the single-channel fluid domain, exactly as the paper's own simplified model: a rectangular prism w x b x 25.4 mm, for each of the five cases (194x884, 229x1250, 300x1520, 339x1895, 534x2910 um, all 25400 um long). Square corners, constant cross-section, no taper, no fillets. That is enough to reproduce the paper's thin-wall (H1) results, which are the ones that match the experiment to 5.2 per cent, and it is the geometry the validated 20 x 50 x 100 quarter-domain grid was built on. The quarter domain is w/2 x b/2 x 25.4 mm.

NOT BUILDABLE - the 3D conjugate half-domain of Fig. 4(a) and the full ten-channel heat sink. Exactly what is missing:
1. ww, the channel wall (fin) thickness. It is defined in the Nomenclature and drawn in Fig. 3, but no number is given anywhere. Without it there is no pitch, no half-fin width for the Fig. 4(a) solid, and no spanwise extent for the ten-channel array. This is the single blocking dimension.
2. The real copper thickness beneath the channel floor. Only the CFD value is given, and the paper itself calls it arbitrary ("chosen (somewhat arbitrarily) to be 1.5 mm"). Use 1.5 mm to reproduce their CFD; do not use it as a measurement of the hardware.
3. Which of the 25.4 / 25.4 / 70 mm block dimensions is the flow direction. The paper states L = 25.4 mm and base area = L^2, so the heated footprint is 25.4 x 25.4 mm, but it never says where the 70 mm lies relative to the channels.
4. All inlet/outlet plenum and port geometry and positions, the cartridge-heater hole diameters/positions, and the acrylic lid thickness.
5. Channel corner radius, saw-kerf floor profile and surface roughness.

DO NOT measure ww off Fig. 3 (captioned "not to scale") and do not back it out of "10 channels in a 25.4 mm block" - the paper never says the array spans the full block face, so that would be an invented number. I also checked the companion pressure-drop paper (Liu and Garimella, AIAA J. Thermophys. Heat Transfer 18 (2004) 65-72) via the Purdue repository and could not obtain a fin width from it either; its public record is abstract-only.

DOMAIN SPLIT for the conjugate case, as the paper defines it: FLUID = w/2 wide x b tall x 25.4 mm long (half channel, symmetry plane on the channel centreline). SOLID = a half-fin column of width ww/2 (UNKNOWN) and height b on one side, sitting on a substrate slab of thickness t = 1.5 mm that spans the full domain width (ww/2 + w/2). Boundary conditions that fix the orientation: top face adiabatic (it is the plastic lid), bottom face uniform heat flux, both side faces symmetry. Heat enters the fluid on three sides only - the heat transfer area per channel is stated as L(w + 2b), i.e. floor plus two side walls, top excluded.
specs.operating_point:
FLUID: deionized water, single phase, liquid. Treated in the CFD as "incompressible and Newtonian, with constant thermophysical properties over the range of temperatures considered (22-70 degC)". No density, viscosity, k or cp values are tabulated; Prandtl number is given as Pr = 5.0 for the present work in Table 5. Water thermal conductivity in the Nusselt reduction was "evaluated at the mean fluid temperature, Tm". The loop also carries a 7 um filter upstream of the flowmeter.

FLOW RATE: "A needle valve downstream of the pressure tank allows fine adjustment of the flow rate from 0.1 to 2.2 l/min, which corresponds to a Reynolds number range of 300-3500." This is the total flow through the test section (all ten channels), measured by a flowmeter "calibrated using a digital scale and stopwatch". Per-channel flow rate and channel velocity are NOT_STATED. Flow is driven by pressurized nitrogen gas on a holding tank, not a pump.

REYNOLDS NUMBER: nominal range 300-3500, based on channel hydraulic diameter. "The experiments were conducted over the nominal Reynolds number range of 300-3500." Laminar-to-transition break observed at Re ~ 1500-2000: "Beyond a range of Reynolds number of approximately 1500-2000, the experimental results show a change in slope, reflecting a transition from laminar flow." All numerical work was laminar only: "Only flow rates in the laminar regime were considered."

HEAT FLUX: "An average heat flux at the base of q'' ~= 45 W/cm2 is maintained in the experiments", defined on the L^2 = 25.4 x 25.4 mm base area. Four cartridge heaters, 800 W combined maximum. Worked example given: "out of the 325.2 W of power dissipated by the cartridge heaters in Test #1 (at Re = 1596), 286.2 W was transferred to the coolant", with "In general, 85-90% of the power provided to the cartridge heaters was transferred to the water."

SPECIFIC OPERATING POINTS NAMED IN THE PAPER:
- Grid-independence and Figs. 5/6 point: Test #1 (w = 194 um, b = 884 um), Re = 1100.
- Energy-balance example: Test #1, Re = 1596, 325.2 W in / 286.2 W to coolant.
- Table 5 entrance-length cases, present work: Dh = 318 um, L = 25.4 mm, Re = 300 (x+ = 0.266, Lent,hyd/L = 0.19) and Re = 1500 (x+ = 0.053, Lent,hyd/L = 0.94); and Dh = 903 um, L = 25.4 mm, Re = 300 (x+ = 0.0938, Lent,hyd/L = 0.53) and Re = 1800 (x+ = 0.0156, Lent,hyd/L = 3.20). All with water, Pr = 5.0, fluid temperature range 22-70 degC. CAUTION: in the printed Table 5 the last two present-work rows show "534" in the Dh column; that is a typo for the Test #5 channel WIDTH. Back-calculating x+ = L/(Dh*Re) = 25400/(903*300) = 0.0938 confirms the intended Dh is 903 um, not 534 um.

CFD BOUNDARY/INLET CONDITIONS: "At the inlet, a fully developed velocity profile was specified for thermally developing flow simulations, while a uniform inlet velocity profile was used for simultaneously developing flow simulations. An outflow boundary condition was specified at the exit in both cases." Top adiabatic, two sides symmetry, bottom uniform heat flux (conjugate model). The paper concludes thermally developing (hydrodynamically developed) is the correct assumption for its experiment, because with real inlet/exit manifolds the development length collapsed to "Lent,h/L ~= 0.04 for Re = 300" versus 0.188 for a uniform inlet profile.

MEASUREMENT UNCERTAINTY: Nusselt number 6-17 per cent; temperatures +/-0.3 degC; channel dimensions +/-15 um; wall-temperature extrapolation error less than 1 per cent; heat-flux-from-gradient method rejected because its uncertainty "can be as large as 15% due to heat losses along the sides of the copper block".
specs.reported_results:
THE 5 PER CENT AGREEMENT STATEMENT, verbatim from the abstract: "Numerical predictions obtained based on a classical, continuum approach were found to be in good agreement with the experimental data (showing an average deviation of 5%), suggesting that a conventional analysis approach can be employed in predicting heat transfer behavior in microchannels of the dimensions considered in this study. However, the entrance and boundary conditions imposed in the experiment need to be carefully matched in the predictive approaches."

Its source in the body, Section 4.2: "The average deviation between the experiments and the computational results for the thermally developing state for all five test geometries is 5.5% for results from [21] and 5.2% for the present results, as detailed in Table 6."

TABLE 6 - "Difference between experimental results and numerical predictions (for H1, thermally developing conditions)", footnote "Based on results for Re < 1500". Columns: Test #, w (um), Deviation from [21] (Wibulswas) %, Deviation from present numerical predictions (thin wall model) %.
  Test 1, w = 194 um: 3.4 +/- 2.1 | 6.5 +/- 3.5
  Test 2, w = 229 um: 8.1 +/- 5.6 | 4.7 +/- 3.1
  Test 3, w = 300 um: 6.1 +/- 4.9 | 4.5 +/- 3.4
  Test 4, w = 339 um: 4.4 +/- 3.6 | 7.7 +/- 3.7
  Test 5, w = 534 um: 5.5 +/- 3.0 | 2.4 +/- 1.5
  Mean:               5.5 +/- 1.8 | 5.2 +/- 2.0
(Means check out: (3.4+8.1+6.1+4.4+5.5)/5 = 5.5; (6.5+4.7+4.5+7.7+2.4)/5 = 5.16.)

HARD NUSSELT NUMBERS A SIMULATION CAN BE CHECKED AGAINST (the only Nu values printed as numbers for the present geometry; all at Test #1, w = 194 um, b = 884 um, Re = 1100):
  Full 3D conjugate model: Nu = 8.82 (grid 40x128x80), 9.05 (50x160x100), 9.00 (60x192x120).
  Simplified thin-wall (H1) model, quarter domain: Nu = 8.78 (16x40x80), 8.87 (20x50x100), 8.97 (24x60x120).
Everything else is plotted, not tabulated. Figs. 7-11 give experimental Nu vs Re for the 194, 229, 300, 339 and 534 um channels against Wibulswas [21] TD/SD, present thin-wall TD, present 3D conjugate TD and Gnielinski turbulent; Fig. 5 compares the four numerical treatments for 194 um over Re = 500-3000 on a Nu axis of 5-25. No Nu-vs-Re data table is published, so those curves would have to be digitised if needed - I am not reporting read-off values as data.

BOUNDARY-CONDITION SENSITIVITY (useful as a model-choice check): "results in Fig. 5 obtained using a uniform heat flux boundary condition deviate by a 12.4% standard deviation from the full conjugate analysis, compared to a smaller deviation of 7.1% for the uniform temperature boundary condition... predictions from the thin-wall approximation are in excellent agreement with the 3D conjugate analysis, deviating by less than 1.3%."

HEAT TRANSFER COEFFICIENT: Fig. 12 plots h (W/m2K) against x* for all five hydraulic diameters (318, 387, 501, 575, 902 um as legended), h axis running to 25000 W/m2K, with dashed trend-line fits. Only comparative statement given numerically: "the heat transfer coefficients for the smallest microchannel (w = 194 lm) are almost three times the values for the largest microchannel (w = 534 lm) over the overlapping x* range in the figure."

TURBULENT/TRANSITIONAL REGIME: experiments extend to Re = 3500; "the experimental Nusselt numbers are generally higher in this turbulent region than predictions from correlations in [15,16,28]", while Petukhov and Dittus-Boelter lie above the data. No new correlation is proposed by this paper.

FRICTION FACTOR AND PRESSURE DROP: NOT_STATED. The rig has the instrumentation - "A differential pressure transducer with a carrier demodulator is used to measure the pressure drop across the test section" and Fig. 2(b) shows pressure taps - but this paper publishes no measured dP, no f values and no f-Re plot. The friction factor f appears only inside the quoted Petukhov and Gnielinski turbulent Nusselt correlations in Table 3, i.e. f = (1.82 ln(Re) - 1.64)^-2. The pressure-drop data set is the companion paper: "The present work complements the detailed flow field and pressure drop measurements of Liu and Garimella [10]" (D. Liu, S.V. Garimella, Investigation of liquid flow in microchannels, AIAA J. Thermophys. Heat Transfer 18 (2004) 65-72, Dh 244-974 um, Re 230-6500).

JUNCTION / WALL TEMPERATURE: no junction temperature is reported (this is a copper test block, not a chip). Wall temperature is obtained by extrapolation, Tw = T4 - (s*q''/kCu) with s = 3.18 mm. Fig. 6(a) plots the local side-wall temperature for the 194 um channel at Re = 1100 over a wall-temperature axis of 330-350 K and an axial axis 0-0.02+ m; Fig. 6(b) plots the corresponding local side-wall heat flux over 0 to 4E+06 W/m2. Neither is tabulated. The CFD property range quoted is 22-70 degC.

CONTEXT TABLE (not this paper's own data): Table 2 reproduces Wibulswas's Nux vs x* for rectangular ducts at constant heat flux for alpha <= 0.1, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0 and >= 10.0 - the reference curves their results are compared against. Table 3 lists the eleven conventional correlations used (Kays and Crawford fully developed, Sieder-Tate, Stephan, Shah and London, Hausen, Dittus-Boelter, Petukhov, Gnielinski, Adams). Table 4 summarises prior microchannel studies. Table 5 gives entrance lengths.
specs.mesh_used:
TWO SEPARATE MESHES, both FLUENT 6 (reference [23], "FLUENT 6 User's Guide, Lebanon, NH, Fluent Inc., 2000"). Schemes: "The convective and conductive terms were discretized using first-order upwind and second-order central-difference schemes, respectively."

1) FULL 3D CONJUGATE MODEL (fluid + copper substrate, half-domain of Fig. 4(a)):
"The entire computational domain was discretized using a 50 x 160 x 100 (x-y-z) grid."
Grid-convergence study, smallest microchannel (w = 194 um, b = 884 um) at Re = 1100: average Nu = 8.82, 9.05 and 9.00 for 40x128x80, 50x160x100 and 60x192x120 respectively. "The predicted average Nusselt number changed by 2.6% from the first to the second mesh, and only by 0.5% upon further refinement to the finest grid. Hence the intermediate (50 x 160 x 100) grid was used in the fluid domain for the results presented in this work."
Total cells: 50 x 160 x 100 = 800,000.

2) SIMPLIFIED / THIN-WALL (H1) MODEL - this is the grid referred to in the task brief:
"Utilizing symmetry conditions, only a quarter of the domain was modeled. A uniform mesh was used along the channel width and height, while the mesh in the channel length direction had a successive ratio of 1.08. For the microchannels considered in this study, with a nominal aspect ratio of 5, a computational grid of 20 x 50 x 100 cells was found to be adequate for the quarter domain shown in Fig. 4(b)."
Grid-convergence study, same case (w = 194 um, b = 884 um, Re = 1100): average Nu = 8.78, 8.87 and 8.97 for 16x40x80, 20x50x100 and 24x60x120 respectively. "As the difference in Nusselt numbers between the two finer meshes was only 1.1%, the 20 x 50 x 100 mesh was considered sufficiently accurate for the present computations."
Total cells: 20 x 50 x 100 = 100,000. Quarter domain = w/2 x b/2 x L, fluid only, no solid; all four channel walls carry the thin highly-conductive zero-axial-conduction wall that realises H1.

AXIAL GRADING: successive ratio 1.08 in the streamwise direction, on the quarter-domain mesh (100 cells over 25.4 mm). The paper does not state whether the grading is one-sided from the inlet or symmetric, and does not state the first-cell size.

CELL TYPE: NOT_STATED explicitly. The counts are given as structured i-j-k triples (20 x 50 x 100, 50 x 160 x 100), which implies a structured hexahedral mesh, but the paper never uses the words hexahedral, structured or tetrahedral. MESHER: NOT_STATED (FLUENT 6 is named as the solver only; no mention of GAMBIT or any other preprocessor). y+ / near-wall treatment: NOT_STATED (all CFD is laminar). No GCI, Richardson extrapolation or order-of-convergence estimate is reported - grid independence is argued only from the per cent change in average Nu between successive meshes quoted above.

specs.buildable:
YES for the fluid domain and the two-level intersection - this is the most completely dimensioned MMC I could read, and the two levels close against each other arithmetically - but you must supply FOUR numbers the paper does not state. Read this section before modelling.

HOW THE TWO LEVELS CONNECT (quoted, since this was the hard part of the brief):
The device is two bonded silicon wafers. Fig. 1 caption: "Conceptual design of an in-chip scale embedded microchannel-3D manifold cooler: the blue arrow depicts fluid flow and distribution of cold liquid through multiple inlet micro-conduits, followed by a 90° turn to enter the cold plate microchannels, exchanging heat in a direct impingement flow configuration ..., followed by an 180° U-turn to exit through the adjacent outlet micro-conduits of the manifold". The manifold conduits run CROSSWISE over the channels: "the fluid is divided into two streams at the intersections between the manifold inlet micro-conduits and the cold plate microchannels that are perpendicular to the direction to the manifold micro-conduits". The companion ASME paper spells the same path out step by step: "The fluid is supplied through the fluid inlet openings (1) from the backside of the manifold substrate and it is uniformly distributed within the inlet plenums (2). The distributed fluid passes the gradual contraction region (between 2 and 3) and keeps flowing through the inlet conduits (3) until it reaches to the intersections between the manifold inlet conduits and the CP microchannels (between 3 and 4). At the intersection, the fluid is diverged and the partial fluid moves toward the CP microchannels' heated section by making a 90 deg-turn. The diverged fluid proceeds along the CP microchannels and heat is transferred from the CP microchannels' surface to the fluid until it exits through the adjacent manifold outlet conduits (4) by making another 90 deg turn. The nondiverged fluid at the intersection keeps flowing along the manifold inlet conduits until it reaches to the next intersection and the same flow pattern as described earlier is repeated."
Which face each feature is etched from (this fixes the solid): Fig. 2 caption - "As the inlet plenums and inlet micro-conduits are interconnected, these features were protected by a thin Al layer while exit micro-conduits and holes for fluid inlet supply were etched from the backside." Fig. 3 caption - "Microchannels and other microscale features were anisotropically etched in the cold plate and the 3D manifold substrates. Double-sided anisotropic Si etch technique was used to define the microstructures with different etch depth in the 3D manifold." Hmani,out (1000 um) equals the full manifold wafer thickness, so the outlet conduits are through-etched and vent out of the manifold back face; the inlet conduits are 700 um deep from the bond face, leaving a 300 um silicon cap above them, and are fed sideways from the inlet plenum through the gradual-contraction region. Bond layer: Au-Si eutectic, 410-420 degC.

SO: the fluid domain you can build without guessing is - a 25-channel field at 200 um pitch (150 um wide x 75 um deep, 50 um fins), overlaid at 90 degrees by 6 inlet conduits 150 um wide x 700 um tall alternating with outlet conduits 520 um wide x 1000 um tall, separated by 81 um walls, on an 832 um manifold pitch. Every channel/conduit crossing is an open 150 x 150 um window where the two levels merge.

WHAT IS MISSING (supply these or the solid will not be watertight / will not match the paper):
1. Microchannel length. NOT_STATED. The heated region is 5 x 5 mm and the 6 inlet/outlet pairs span 4992 um, so 5000 um is the only length consistent with the paper, but it is my arithmetic, not a quote. Decide this explicitly before cutting the channel field.
2. Number of outlet micro-conduits. NOT_STATED (only "6 inlets" is stated). 6 is what closes the 5 mm edge. Assume 6 inlet + 6 outlet alternating.
3. dbase, the silicon left under the channel floor. NOT_STATED in this paper. Use 425 um, which the companion ASME paper states for the identical cold plate ("thick Si bulk layer, 425 µm") and which equals 500 um wafer minus 75 um channel depth.
4. hmani,plen = 12.5 with NO UNIT in Table 1. Every other row in that table carries mm or um; this one does not. 12.5 mm is larger than the whole device, 12.5 um is implausibly thin, so the plenum vertical dimension is genuinely unresolved from the text. Resolve it from the publisher's Fig. 2(b) before modelling the plenum, or model the plenum as a 4 mm-radius x 1.45 mm-long cavity and treat its height as a free parameter.
ALSO NOT_STATED and therefore not buildable to the paper: the outer die footprint of either wafer (only the 5 x 5 mm heated square and the 52 mm2 heater-trace footprint are given), and the pin-fin arrays in the entrance/exit plenums (their existence is stated, no pin diameter/height/pitch/count anywhere).

VERIFICATION - I checked this geometry twice, as asked:
Pass 1, source fidelity. I did not trust pdftotext layout mode, which interleaved Table 1's label and value columns and shifted Rmani,plen / Lmani,plen / hmani,plen by one row. I re-extracted the table with PyMuPDF word coordinates and read the x-position of every token, which gave the correct label-value pairing above and also exposed the missing unit on hmani,plen. The abstract, Fig. 1/2/3 captions and the nomenclature were extracted the same way. Caution for anyone re-reading these PDFs: the Elsevier font maps the micro sign to the letter "l", so the raw text shows "75 lm" where the paper prints "75 um".
Pass 2, geometric closure and cross-source agreement. (a) Channel level: 25 x 150 + 24 x 50 = 4950 um, plus a 25 um half-fin at each edge = 5000 um, exactly the stated 5 x 5 mm2 heated area. (b) Manifold level: 6 x 150 + 6 x 520 + 12 x 81 = 4992 um, the same 5 mm edge to within 8 um. Both levels are therefore commensurate and the 6-inlet/6-outlet reading is right. (c) Solid: 500 um cold-plate wafer minus 75 um channel depth = 425 um, which is independently stated as 425 um in the companion ASME paper - two papers agreeing on a number neither derives from the other. (d) The companion ASME variant closes even harder on its own numbers: 4 x 250 + 4 x 830 + 8 x 85 = 5000 um exactly, on the identical 25-channel / 75 x 150 um cold plate. Four independent closures, no contradictions found. The only internal defect I found in the primary paper is the unitless hmani,plen.

specs.mesh_used:
PRIMARY PAPER (Jung et al., IJHMT 130, 2019): conjugate (solid+fluid) CFD in ANSYS Fluent 16.0.0, "single-phase conjugate numerical simulations (ANSYS Fluent 16.0.0)", built on "the exact micro-cooler geometry (Table 1)". Grid convergence was done properly and is quoted: "A mesh size independence study is conducted with four different number of mesh elements, from 1.11E6 to 10.9E6, and the results are plotted in Fig. A.II.2. There is less than 0.31% change in the average heater temperature, Theater,avg, and 1.7% change in the total pressure drop, DPtotal, if the number of mesh element is higher than 3.19E6. Therefore, the number of mesh element used in this study was 5.39E6 based on the mesh independence study." The four levels are named explicitly: "The number of mesh elements used in the study are from 1.11E6 to 3.19E6 to 5.40E6 to 1.09E7", run at "Tin = 293 K, Qin = 0.001 kg/s, q'' = 4,494,517 W/m2". So: FINAL MESH 5.39E6 cells (5.4 million), converged within 0.31% on temperature and 1.7% on pressure drop above 3.19E6 cells. Separate solid and fluid domains were meshed (Fig. A.II.1: "(a) Solid and (b) fluid domains for the conjugate numerical analysis"). CELL TYPE: NOT_STATED. Turbulence/laminar model: NOT_STATED for this paper (channel Re is 40-122, i.e. laminar). Near-wall layer treatment: NOT_STATED.

COMPANION ASME PAPER (Jung et al., J. Electron. Packag. 142(3) 031117, 2020), same device family, for cross-reference: "The experimental results are validated by conjugate numerical simulations, ANSYS FLUENT 18.1 (Canonsburg, PA), for the exact EMMC geometry (Table 1). ... The number of mesh elements varies from 5 to 32 × 106, and the results are plotted in Fig. 11. There are less than 0.6% change in the average and maximum heater temperature, and the total pressure drop if the number of mesh elements is more than 25 × 106. ... Therefore, we have used 25 × 106 of mesh elements in this study." Its solver conditions (Table 7, "Thermofluidic and solver conditions for mesh independence study"): supplied heat flux 4.464E6 W/m2, mass flow rate 8.263E-3 kg/s, inlet temperature 2.981E2 K, solver model "SST k-omega (turbulent)". Cell type again NOT_STATED.

Note the order-of-magnitude gap between the two: 5.4E6 cells for the water device versus 25E6 cells for the R-245fa device on effectively the same geometry. If you are sizing a mesh for a rebuild, 25E6 is the better-converged target (0.6% on all three monitored quantities) and the SST k-omega choice is the one the group justified for capturing the 90-degree turns at the conduit/channel intersections.

specs.buildable:
YES for the array and its enclosing silicon shell — this is an unusually well-closed geometry. NO for the inlet/outlet ports and the die outline.

WHAT IS FULLY DETERMINED (watertight solid + watertight fluid domain):
Fluid domain = a 6600 x 14400 x 300 um rectangular box, minus 264 pin-equivalents of 300 um diameter right circular cylinders spanning the full 300 um height. Solid domain = 200 um substrate below + 500 um cover above + the pins + the 150 um edge walls, all silicon, bonded (no interface gap: silicon-to-silicon direct bonding).

THE LAYOUT IS NOT GUESSED — IT IS FORCED AND TRIPLE-CHECKED. The paper states the array width (6.6 mm), length (14.4 mm), pitch (600 um), diameter (300 um) and row count (24) but never prints the column count. Three independent arithmetic checks against numbers the paper does print pin it down exactly:
  CHECK 1, minimum flow area. Paper states A_min = 0.99 mm2. A row of 10 full pins + 2 half-pins at the walls gives (6.6 - (10*0.3 + 2*0.15)) * 0.3 = 0.9900 mm2. An offset row of 11 full pins gives (6.6 - 11*0.3) * 0.3 = 0.9900 mm2. Both match exactly, so the transverse pitch tiles the 6.6 mm width with no leftover.
  CHECK 2, inline convection area. Paper states 231.72 mm2. Taking 24 identical rows of 10 full + 2 wall-bisected half pins: 2*(6.6*14.4 - 264*pi*0.15^2) + 264*pi*0.3*0.3 + (2*14.4*0.3 - 48*0.3*0.3) = 231.7221 mm2. Matches to 5 significant figures.
  CHECK 3, staggered convection area. Paper states 233.88 mm2. Taking 12 wall-rows alternating with 12 offset rows of 11 pins: same base and pin-side terms, sidewalls cut by only 24 half-pins instead of 48, giving 233.8821 mm2. Matches to 5 significant figures.
  CHECK 2b, the reference channel sink. Paper states 190.08 mm2; 11 * 14.4 * (2*0.3 + 2*0.3) = 190.0800 mm2 exactly, which independently confirms the 300 um channel depth taken from the layer thickness, the 11 channels, and four-sided (all-wall) heating.
Because checks 2 and 3 land on the paper's own published areas to 5 significant figures under one single consistent interpretation, the pin count (264 pin-equivalents), the pin height (300 um), and the half-pins embedded in the sidewalls are confirmed rather than assumed.

WHAT IS MISSING, and it does block a complete chip model:
  1. Inlet and outlet hole diameter — NOT_STATED. The holes are laser-drilled through the 500 um cover, so they are top-fed, but no diameter exists anywhere in the text.
  2. Inlet and outlet hole position — NOT_STATED. No coordinates.
  3. Any inlet/outlet plenum or distributor — NOT_STATED. There may be none (flow may enter the array directly under the hole), but the paper does not say.
  4. Overall die footprint — NOT_STATED. Only the array is dimensioned. The die is necessarily larger (bond pads, cover holes) but its outline is never given.
  5. Pin draft angle and root fillet — NOT_STATED. Model as right cylinders with sharp roots; the paper only asserts high perpendicularity from DRIE.
  6. Stagger offset as a printed number — NOT_STATED, but unambiguous in words ("in the middle of the two adjacent micro pin fins in the front row"), so 300 um, exactly half the quoted 600 um pitch.

RECOMMENDED BUILD, and the caveat that comes with it. Build the array as the full 6600 x 14400 x 300 um box with flat inlet and outlet faces at y = 0 and y = 14400 um, sandwiched by the 200 um and 500 um silicon plates. That is watertight and defensible. But be aware the measured pressure drop was taken at ports upstream and downstream of the chip ("A temperature port and a pressure port are installed at both the inlet and the outlet of the test chip"), so it includes the laser-drilled hole losses and the 90-degree turn into the array. A box-inlet model will therefore UNDER-predict the reported dP. Nusselt number and thermal resistance are referenced to the array itself and to the quoted A_c, so those two are directly comparable to a box-inlet model; pressure drop is not. Do not use the dP numbers as a validation target without modelling the holes, which cannot be done from this paper.
specs.operating_point:
FLUID: deionized water. Quote: "A temperature port and a pressure port are installed at both the inlet and the outlet of the test chip to measure the temperature rise and pressure drop of the working fluid (deionized water)."

INLET TEMPERATURE: 298.15 K (25.0 C). Quote: "The temperature of the thermostatic water tank is kept at 298.15 K with a temperature fluctuation of less than 0.05 K." Fluid property values (rho, mu, cp, k) are NOT_STATED anywhere in the paper — use water at 298.15 K.

REYNOLDS NUMBER RANGE: 79.2 to 882.3. Quote: "Three heat sink structures are tested in the Reynolds number range of 79.2 to 882.3, namely, a microchannel heat sink (MCHS), an inline micro-pin-fin heat sink (I-MPFHS) and a staggered micro-pin-fin heat sink (S-MPFHS)."
Re is defined on the PIN DIAMETER and the MINIMUM free-flow area, not on a hydraulic diameter and not on a frontal area. Quote: "Re = rho*U*L/mu = rho*Q*L/(mu*Amin), where Q is the flow rate, L is the characterized length (the hydraulic diameter for the microchannel heat sink and the fin diameter for the micro pin fin heat sink, both equal to 300 μm), Amin is the minimum vertical cross-sectional area of the flow region (0.99 mm2 for both the microchannel and the micro-pin-fin heat sinks)." Match this definition exactly or your Re will not be theirs.

Specific Re values quoted in the results: 339.3, 678.7 ("under the conditions of Re = 339.3 and Re = 678.7"), 814.4, and the band 271.5 < Re < 542.9. Vortex-shedding transition for the inline array is quoted at Re = 550: "when Re is higher than 550, the flow stability in the separation zones of the inline micro pin fins decreases and the flow structure in the separation zones gradually evolves from a steady vortex pair to an unsteady Kármán vortex street."

HEAT FLUX: 100 W/cm2 per heater. Quote: "Each heater provides a heat flux of 100 W/cm2." Applied on the back of the 200 um substrate only (the heaters are on the substrate backside), over six 2.9 x 4.6 mm pads covering the whole array. Total power is NOT_STATED; 6 * 2.9 * 4.6 mm2 * 100 W/cm2 = 80.04 W is DERIVED from quoted numbers. Note the heating is four-sided in the sense that all four walls of each passage are silicon and conducting, which the paper stresses is the novelty: "most conclusions about the performance of microchannel and micro-pin-fin heat sinks in such literature are based on three-sided heating cases, which use glass as cover plates [23,24,25,26]. Whether these conclusions are applicable to four-sided heating cases has not been systematically studied."

FLOW RATE AND VELOCITY: NOT_STATED. No absolute Q or velocity appears in the paper; only the uncertainty "Flow rate, Q ±0.5%". DERIVED from the quoted Re definition with water at 298.15 K (rho = 997.0 kg/m3, mu = 8.90e-4 Pa s), Q = Re*mu*A_min/(rho*L):
  Re =  79.2  ->  Q = 0.233 mL/s ( 14.0 mL/min), U_max = 0.236 m/s
  Re = 271.5  ->  Q = 0.800 mL/s ( 48.0 mL/min), U_max = 0.808 m/s
  Re = 339.3  ->  Q = 1.000 mL/s ( 60.0 mL/min), U_max = 1.010 m/s
  Re = 542.9  ->  Q = 1.599 mL/s ( 96.0 mL/min), U_max = 1.615 m/s
  Re = 678.7  ->  Q = 1.999 mL/s (120.0 mL/min), U_max = 2.020 m/s
  Re = 814.4  ->  Q = 2.399 mL/s (144.0 mL/min), U_max = 2.423 m/s
  Re = 882.3  ->  Q = 2.599 mL/s (156.0 mL/min), U_max = 2.625 m/s
These land on exact round mL/min values (60.0, 96.0, 120.0, 144.0, 156.0), which is strong evidence the authors set flow rate in round increments and that the recovered Q is right. U_max here is the velocity in the minimum section, Q/A_min, which is the velocity their Re is built on. Flow is laminar-to-transitional; the paper reports unsteady Karman vortex shedding above Re = 550 in the inline array, so a steady RANS run will not capture the inline high-Re behaviour.

EXPERIMENTAL UNCERTAINTIES (quoted table): flow rate +/-0.5%, geometric error +/-1 um, inlet water temperature +/-0.2 K, outlet fluid temperature +/-0.2 K, sensor temperature +/-0.42 K, heater temperature +/-0.45 K, pressure drop +/-4.5% max, Reynolds number +/-0.8% max, Nusselt number +/-5.7% max, thermal resistance +/-5.0% max.
specs.reported_results:
NUSSELT NUMBER (the single cleanest validation target, because the paper gives both the definition and the area it is normalised on):
Quote: "Under the condition of Re = 814.4, Nu of I-MPFHS reaches 11.70, while that of MCHS is only 8.54."
  inline pin fin, Re = 814.4:  Nu = 11.70
  straight channels, Re = 814.4: Nu = 8.54
Nu is built on h = q/(A_c*(T_h_avg - T_f)) with q from an energy balance q = rho*cp*Q*(T_o - T_i), T_f = (T_i + T_o)/2, and the characteristic length 300 um. To compare, you must use their A_c (231.72 mm2 inline, 233.88 mm2 staggered, 190.08 mm2 channels) and their L = 300 um. Staggered Nu is stated to be much higher than both but NO numeric staggered Nu value is given (figure only). Full Nu-vs-Re curves are in Figure 6 only, so no other numbers are extractable from the text.

THERMAL RESISTANCE (K/W), paired with pressure drop. These are the four quoted (theta, dP) points:
  inline    I-MPFHS:  theta = 0.8513 K/W at dP =  1.16 kPa
  channels  MCHS:     theta = 0.8250 K/W at dP =  1.18 kPa
  staggered S-MPFHS:  theta = 0.9613 K/W at dP =  1.12 kPa
  inline    I-MPFHS:  theta = 0.2166 K/W at dP = 27.70 kPa
  staggered S-MPFHS:  theta = 0.2231 K/W at dP = 29.49 kPa
Quote: "When the pressure drop is lower than 1.5 kPa, the cooling capability of I-MPFHS (θ = 0.8513 K/W at ... = 1.16 kPa) is a little higher than MCHS (θ = 0.8250 K/W at ... = 1.18 kPa) and both of them are obviously better than S-MPFHS (θ = 0.9613 K/W at ... = 1.12 kPa) because of the severe endwall effect and high pressure drop in S-MPFHS." And: "when the pressure drop is higher than 20 kPa, the cooling capability of I-MPFHS (θ = 0.2166 K/W at ... = 27.70 kPa) exceeds S-MPFHS (θ = 0.2231 K/W at ... = 29.49 kPa) because of the high heat transfer enhancement and the low pressure drop price brought by the unsteady vortex street in I-MPFHS."
theta is defined as the average temperature rise of the simulated power IC per unit power input: "the average thermal resistance (θ) represents the average temperature rise of the simulated power IC per unit power input."

PRESSURE DROP vs Re: NOT_STATED as a table. Only the five dP values above, each tied to a theta. Quote: "Figure 9 shows variations of the pressure drop with Re." The trend is stated: staggered dP much higher than inline and channels; inline dP similar to channels at low Re, diverging upward as Re rises. Remember the measured dP is port-to-port across the whole chip including the laser-drilled cover holes, so it is NOT directly comparable to an array-only CFD dP (see the buildable field).

JUNCTION TEMPERATURE: NOT_STATED. No absolute junction or wall temperatures are given. Only thermal resistance and relative centreline temperature profiles (Figure 8), described qualitatively: "the maximum temperature difference of MCHS is about twice the value of S-MPFHS at Re = 339.3, while it is about triple at Re = 678.7." The upstream/downstream split used in that discussion is quoted as 0 to 7.2 mm and 7.2 to 14.4 mm.

HEADLINE CONCLUSION: "I-MPFHS shows the most effective cooling capability when the rated pressure drop of the pump is lower than 1.5 kPa or higher than 20 kPa and S-MPFHS has the most effective cooling capability when the rated pressure drop of the pump is in the range of 1.5 to 20 kPa."
specs.mesh_used:
NOT_STATED — there is no mesh, no cell count, no mesher and no grid-convergence study, because this is a purely experimental paper. There is no CFD model in it at all. The only numerical-flavoured content is the data-reduction algebra (Equations 1 to 7) and a Moffat-style uncertainty propagation.

The paper does cite prior numerical work on circular micro-pin-fin arrays ("Both experimental and numerical studies on circular micro-pin-fin heat sinks show that staggered micro-pin-fin heat sinks have a much higher Nusselt number than inline micro-pin-fin heat sinks"), so meshing precedent would have to come from those references (notably Mohammadi and Kosar, J. Therm. Anal. Calorim. 2019, 140:1057-1068, doi 10.1007/s10973-019-08840-2, and Mohammadi and Kosar, J. Heat Transf. 2017, 139:062402, doi 10.1115/1.4035655), not from this paper.

MESHING GUIDANCE IMPLIED BY THE GEOMETRY RATHER THAN QUOTED: the smallest fluid gap is 300 um between adjacent pin surfaces and 150 um from the outermost pin surface to each sidewall, while the pin diameter and height are both 300 um, so the aspect ratios are benign and near-cubic. The two real mesher stresses are (a) the 24 half-cylinders tangent to each sidewall in the inline case and 12 per wall in the staggered case, which are the geometric features most likely to produce slivers, and (b) the 264 cylinder-to-plate root intersections top and bottom. The paper reports unsteady Karman vortex shedding above Re = 550 in the inline array, so a validation run there needs a transient solver and a wake-resolving mesh, not a steady one.

Goodson, "Numerical Study of Large Footprint (24 x 24 mm2) Silicon-Based Embedded Microchannel Three-Dimensional Manifold Coolers," ASME J. Electron. specs.buildable:
PARTIALLY. The cooled core is fully buildable and watertight; the feed/plenum region is not.

WHAT YOU CAN BUILD RIGHT NOW, WATERTIGHT, WITH NOTHING INFERRED: the complete 5 mm x 5 mm cooled block, both domains. Cold plate: 200 channels of 10 um width x 75 um depth on a 25 um pitch (design D9), under a 200 um silicon roof, channel length 5 mm. Manifold beneath it: 6 inlet conduits 217 um wide x 700 um deep alternating with 6 outlet conduits 215 um wide x 1000 um deep, separated by 200 um silicon walls, on an 832 um pair pitch, running perpendicular to the cold-plate channels. Every one of those numbers is printed in Table 1, Table 2 or the Fig. 1(b) dimension labels.

THE GEOMETRY SELF-VALIDATES, WHICH IS WHY I TRUST IT. Four independent arithmetic closures all come out exact, with no rounding: (a) channel pitch x channel count = 5000 um for all four cold-plate variants (25x200, 50x100, 100x50, 200x25); (b) the paper's own tabulated wetted area Awet = 5.625, 6.25, 8.5, 17 x 10-5 m2 for D6-D9 reproduces exactly as Ncp x (2*Hcp + 2*Wcp) x 5 mm, which independently pins the channel length at 5 mm and confirms Hcp = 75 um; (c) the tabulated hydraulic diameters 100, 60, 17.65, 17.65 um reproduce exactly from the tabulated Wcp and Hcp; (d) the tabulated Lflow = 416 um and Wmani,wall/Lflow = 24.04 / 48.08 per cent reproduce exactly for both manifolds, and 6 conduit pairs x 832 um = 4992 um fills the 5 mm side. A transcription error would break at least one of these; none break.

WHAT IS MISSING AND BLOCKS A COMPLETE DEVICE MODEL - five items, all NOT_STATED:
1. Au heater thickness and the serpentine trace layout. You cannot build the heater solid. Workaround that stays honest: drop the Au body entirely and apply 800 W/cm2 as a uniform flux on the top face of the cold-plate silicon. That changes the near-surface spreading slightly but nothing in the fluid domain.
2. Manifold floor thickness beneath the 1000 um outlet conduits. Pick any value and state it as your own assumption; it is adiabatic in the paper's boundary conditions, so it does not affect the answer.
3. Overall die footprint. The silicon extends past the 5 x 5 mm cooled square to carry the plenums; no outer dimension is printed.
4. Inlet plenum (semicircular) and outlet opening (square) dimensions. None given.
5. Inlet/outlet port diameters and their positions. None given.

CONSEQUENCE FOR CFD: items 3, 4 and 5 mean you cannot reproduce the paper's reported TOTAL pressure drop, because dP1 (inlet opening to end of plenum) and dP4 (outlet conduit ends to exit opening) depend on geometry the paper never dimensions. You CAN reproduce dP3, the pressure drop across the active cooling region, which is the dominant term in the aggressive designs: Table 8 gives dP3 = 76.6 of 79.3 kPa for D8 and 34.2 of 36.9 kPa for D9, i.e. 93 per cent of the total. So a cooled-core-only model is a legitimate validation target for D8 and D9; it is not for D6, where dP3 is only 2.2 of 5.1 kPa.

IF YOU WANT THE MISSING MANIFOLD HEIGHTS FROM A SECOND SOURCE: Piazza et al., ITHERM 2020, Table I, same design family, explicitly built on design D7 of this paper, gives length 5/10/20 mm, hCP 200 um, wCP,channel 50 um, wCP,wall 50 um, hCP,channel 75 um, t_heater 200 um, hMF 1000 um, hMF,in 750 um, wMF,in 215 um, wMF,wall 200 um, wMF,out 217 um. Note it agrees with this paper on hMF = 1000 um but says 750 um where Fig. 1(b) here says 0.7 mm, and it swaps the 215/217 labels between inlet and outlet. Treat it as a separate paper, not a patch.
specs.operating_point:
Single operating point for the whole parametric study, from Table 3 "Simulation conditions" verbatim:
- Mass flow rate at zone 0: "8.3 x 10-3 kg/s or 0.2 l/min at 25 C"
- Heat fluxes at the heated surfaces: 800 W/cm2
- Energy/viscous model: On/laminar
- Fluid inlet temperature: 298.15 K
- Au thermal conductivity: 298 W/m K
- Si thermal conductivity: 130 W/m K
- Water thermal conductivity: "Piecewise-linear, temperature dependent"

Applied heat flux as a boundary condition: "A constant heat flux, 11,985,378 W/m2, is applied at the top surface of the Au bodies to supply 800 W/cm2 on the 5 x 5 mm2 hot spot. All other solid outer walls are set to be adiabatic."
Outlet: "Zero gauge-pressure condition is applied on the bottom surface of the fluid outlet."
Symmetry: "The cut surfaces along the symmetry lines in the solid and fluid domains are set to be symmetric." Quarter model, two symmetry planes.
Why this point: "For practical considerations, the heat flux of 800 W/cm2 and the flow rate of 0.2 lit/min are chosen to ensure that there will be no two-phase heat transfer, and that the overall pressure drop for the most aggressive design, D8, will stay below 100 kPa."

Reynolds numbers in the microchannels (Table 11, "Renumber (u-channel)"): D4 170, D5 150, D6 150, D7 130, D8 92, D9 46. Fully laminar throughout.

WARNING - THE PAPER'S OWN FLOW NUMBER IS INTERNALLY INCONSISTENT AND YOU MUST NOT COPY IT BLIND. Table 3 prints "8.3 x 10-3 kg/s or 0.2 l/min at 25 C" as if the two were equal. They are not: 0.2 l/min of water at 25 C is about 3.3 x 10-3 kg/s, not 8.3 x 10-3 kg/s. The quantity in Table 3 is the inlet condition of the QUARTER-cut domain ("Mass flow rate at zone 0"), and the full device has two inlets, so one quarter should receive one quarter of the device total: 3.32 x 10-3 / 4 = 8.3 x 10-4 kg/s. The digits "8.3" match that quarter exactly, so the printed exponent is almost certainly a typo for 10-4. Fig. 8 independently labels the device-level condition as "Qtotal = 0.2 l/min, q''heater = 800 W/cm2", which supports the 0.2 l/min figure as the device total. RECOMMENDATION: drive the quarter model at 8.3 x 10-4 kg/s (device total 0.2 l/min, 3.32 x 10-3 kg/s) and sanity-check against the paper's reported outlet temperature of 39.2-39.7 C.

Fluid: single-phase deionised water, inlet 25 C / 298.15 K, temperature-dependent piecewise-linear thermal conductivity and temperature-dependent specific heat ("Cp,f is the saturated specific heat of single-phase water that is temperature-dependent"). Density and viscosity treatment NOT_STATED beyond being incompressible and laminar. Solids: silicon 130 W/m K, gold 298 W/m K.

HEADLINE RESULT (abstract, verbatim): "we implemented strategies such as: (i) symmetric distribution of manifold inlet/outlet conduits, (ii) reducing the thickness of cold-plate (CP) substrate, and (iii) increasing fluid-solid interfacial area in CP microchannels, which resulted in a reduction in thermal resistance from 0.1 for baseline design to 0.04 cm2 K/W, while the pressure drop increased from 8 to 37 kPa."

KEY STEP-BY-STEP CLAIMS (body text, verbatim):
- D4 to D5 (manifold symmetry): "When the inlet/outlet conduits are symmetrically placed in the EMMC, the dPtotal for D5 design is reduced by 38.0% from baseline design D4" and "dP2 contributes to 96% of reduction in dPtotal."
- D5 to D6 (thinner cold plate): "the silicon chip thickness was reduced from 500 to 200 um that resulted in a reduction in thermal resistance to 0.075 cm2 K/W."
- D6 to D7 to D8 (narrower channels): "As the Ncp is doubled from D6 to D7, and from D7 to D8, the Rtotal linearly decreases by 13.0% and 33.8%, respectively."
- D8 to D9 (thinner fins): "we achieved nearly a factor of 2 improvement in pressure drop, from 80 kPa (D8) to 35 kPa (D9), and about 7% reduction in thermal resistance from Rtotal = 0.044 cm2 K/W (D8) to Rtotal = 0.041 cm2 K/W (D9)."
- Conduction/advection floor: "Rconv is the only parameter that decreases with increasing number of Ncp, while Rcond and Radv remain constant (lower limit of 0.034 cm2 K/W)."
- Thermal-resistance split in the baseline: "In the baseline EMMC design, the Rtotal ~ 0.097 cm2 K/W consists of advection (Radv), conduction (Rcond), and convection (Rconv) thermal resistances. For a given heat flux, the advection thermal resistance is fixed and represents ~18% of the total thermal resistance."
- Max vs average temperature: "The difference between average and maximum temperatures for the cases studied here is less than 10%."

ENERGY-BALANCE CAVEAT YOU SHOULD CARRY INTO ANY VALIDATION: "while qtrans and dPtotal changes are less than 1%, even with excessively large number of mesh generated in the computational domain; there is a residual 3% difference between qsupply and qtrans. Therefore, going forward we will use qtrans that translates to less than 3% error in calculations of the Rtotal." So every Rtotal above carries a stated ~3 per cent systematic uncertainty.

EXPERIMENTAL VALIDATION STATUS: not in this paper, but it states "The chosen starting point or the baseline is design D4 since we have already fabricated, conducted tests, and conducted extensive CFD simulations. The CFD results agree well with the experimental data."

The 10 um figure comes from Hazra's 2023 Stanford dissertation describing this family of studies in retrospect: "device simulations in this study and also by Wei et al. [83], Jung et al. [77] and Piazza et al. [78] were all sized ~ 10 um or more to resolve 50 um channels." Treat 4 um as this paper's number and 10 um as the family-level characterisation.

SCALE-UP COST, for context on why the 24 x 24 mm model was hard (Hazra dissertation, verbatim): "Jung et al. had used ~ 23 - 24 million mesh elements to resolve microchannels of width 50 um ... To maintain similar mesh element sizes and resolution near the smallest microchannels, the larger cooler models would require > 70 (100 mm2 cooler) and > 150 (400 mm2 cooler) million mesh elements ... the simulations were finally performed with > 40 (100 mm2) and ~ 65 million (400 mm2) mesh elements with the simulation time of each data point for the large 400 mm2 devices being 3 - 4 days. Simulations of larger 24 x 24 and 25 x 25 mm2 cooler devices proved impossible using the workstation then ... However, an upgraded workstation was later used [83] to accurately model a large 600 mm2 coolers ... this exercise took more than 1 week to complete with the meshing step often crashing the system."
